findings.who: A joint filer who made no 2025 charitable gifts but has a charitable contribution carryover from 2024 because the earlier deduction exceeded the income limits.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only whether they gave in 2025; they truthfully read that as no because all gifts were in an earlier year.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 11, Line 13: "You may have contributions that you couldn't deduct in an earlier year because they exceeded the limits ... enter the amount of your carryover that you are allowed to deduct this year."
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to include a prior-year charitable carryover and ask whether the 2025 charitable deduction, including carryover, is limited, not only whether 2025 gifts were made.

findings.who: A filer who did no cash or property donation but drove 1,000 miles for a charity and claims the 14-cents-per-mile volunteer rate; there is no actual gas or parking receipt.
findings.why_no: They read 'give money or things' and 'spend your own money' as not covering a standard mileage allowance; they say they only drove and gave no money.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 9, Amounts You Can Deduct: "If you drove to and from the volunteer work, you can take the actual cost of gas and oil or 14 cents a mile."
findings.fix: State in the gate that out-of-pocket volunteer costs, including mileage at 14 cents per mile and parking/tolls, count even if no cash was given directly.

findings.who: A filer who let a qualified charity use office space rent-free for 2025 and made no cash or tangible-property gift.
findings.why_no: They truthfully say no because they did not give money or a thing; they gave the use of property, which the gate's wording does not mention.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 10, Limit on the amount you can deduct: "You gave gifts of property that increased in value or gave gifts of the use of property."
findings.fix: Include gifts of property and gifts of the use of property in the gate, or ask broadly whether the filer made any charitable contribution.

findings.who: A filer who gave cash to a qualifying Canadian, Israeli, or Mexican charity, or to a U.S. organization that transfers funds to foreign charities, and knows the general rule that gifts to foreign organizations are not deductible.
findings.why_no: They read the gate's list of charities as U.S. charities and the general foreign-organization rule as a no; they answer no because the funds went to a foreign charity.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 10, Amounts You Can't Deduct: "Gifts to foreign organizations. However, you may be able to deduct gifts to certain U.S. organizations that transfer funds to foreign charities and certain Canadian, Israeli, and Mexican charities."
findings.fix: Add qualifying foreign charities and U.S. organizations that transfer funds abroad to the gate/help, and do not limit the line 11 wording to U.S. charities.

findings.who: A filer who paid a fraternal order an amount that the order used for its charitable purposes, and made no other charitable gifts.
findings.why_no: The gate's examples omit fraternal orders, and the instructions elsewhere say dues or bills paid to lodges and fraternal orders are not deductible; the filer answers no as a dues payment.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 9, Examples of Qualified Charitable Organizations: "Fraternal orders if the gifts will be used for the purposes listed under Gifts to Charity."
findings.fix: Mention fraternal orders when the gift is used for charitable purposes, and distinguish non-deductible dues.

findings.who: A filer who gave cash to a nonprofit scientific research institute or an organization that prevents cruelty to animals, not one of the listed church/school/hospital/veterans/government examples.
findings.why_no: They treat the gate help's list as the whole category of qualifying charities and answer no because their donee is not on the list.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 9, Gifts to Charity: "organizations that are religious, charitable, educational, scientific, or literary in purpose" and "organizations that work to prevent cruelty to children or animals."
findings.fix: Say the examples are not exhaustive and include scientific, literary, and animal-cruelty-prevention organizations.

findings.who: A filer who paid $1,000 to a charity in a state tax-credit program, received a $600 state tax credit, and claims only the remaining $400 as a charitable deduction.
findings.why_no: They see the payment as buying a tax credit or receiving a benefit, not as a gift to charity, so they answer no to the gate.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 10, Amounts You Can't Deduct: "Certain contributions to charitable organizations to the extent that you receive a state or local tax credit in return for your contribution."
findings.fix: Tell filers to count the portion of a state tax-credit payment that is not offset by the credit, and not to treat the whole payment as non-charitable.

findings.who: A filer who pays deductible home mortgage interest to a private lender or seller and receives no Form 1098, so the interest belongs on line 8b, and who used some of the loan proceeds for other purposes.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed only from line 8a. Line 8a is zero because no Form 1098 interest is entered there, so the tool skips the other-use question and treats it as false.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: 'If you paid home mortgage interest to a recipient who didn’t provide you a Form 1098, report your deductible mortgage interest on line 8b.'
findings.fix: Gate on any home mortgage interest on lines 8a, 8b, or 8c, or on having a home mortgage outstanding, not only line 8a > 0.

findings.who: A filer who was liable for and paid mortgage interest and whose share was reported on another borrower’s Form 1098, so the share goes on line 8b, and who used some proceeds for other purposes.
findings.why_no: Line 8a is zero because the Form 1098 is not the filer’s own; the gate never asks the other-use question.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: 'If the shared interest was reported on the other person’s Form 1098, report your share of the interest on line 8b'.
findings.fix: Gate on any home mortgage interest on lines 8a, 8b, or 8c, or on having a home mortgage outstanding, not only line 8a > 0.

findings.who: A filer whose only home mortgage item is points not reported on Form 1098, entered on line 8c, and who used loan proceeds for other purposes.
findings.why_no: Line 8a is zero because the points are on line 8c; the gate treats the other-use question as false.
findings.irs_text: f1040sa p. 1, line 8c: 'Points not reported to you on Form 1098'; i1040sca p. 8: 'Check the box on line 8 if you had one or more home mortgages in 2025 with an outstanding balance and you didn't use all of your home mortgage proceeds from those loans to buy, build, or substantially improve your home.'
findings.fix: Gate on any home mortgage interest or points on lines 8a, 8b, or 8c, or on having a home mortgage outstanding, not only line 8a > 0.

findings.who: A filer who has a Form 1098 home mortgage but used all the borrowed money for other purposes, so the deductible home mortgage interest properly entered on line 8a is zero.
findings.why_no: The gate is line 8a > $0. Because the other-use limit zeroes line 8a, the tool skips the question that would detect the other use and marks it false.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: 'Check the box on line 8 if you had one or more home mortgages in 2025 with an outstanding balance and you didn't use all of your home mortgage proceeds from those loans to buy, build, or substantially improve your home.' Also: 'Interest paid on home mortgage proceeds used for other purposes isn’t deductible on lines 8a or 8b.'
findings.fix: Gate on the existence of a home mortgage with nonqualifying-use potential, not on the deductible line 8a amount; ask the other-use question whenever there is an outstanding home mortgage.

findings.who: A filer with deductible home mortgage interest and other-use proceeds whose line 8a is reduced to zero by the mortgage interest credit on Form 8396, line 3.
findings.why_no: The gate uses the post-credit line 8a amount, which is zero, so the other-use question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: 'If you are claiming the mortgage interest credit ... subtract the amount shown on Form 8396, line 3, from the total deductible interest you paid on your home mortgage. Enter the result on line 8a.'
findings.fix: Use the pre-credit mortgage interest or the existence of the mortgage for the gate; do not let the Form 8396 subtraction zero out the gate.

findings.who: A filer with a home mortgage outstanding in 2025 but no interest paid or entered on line 8a, such as an interest-free family loan, who used some proceeds for other purposes.
findings.why_no: Line 8a is zero because there is no interest; the gate treats the other-use question as false even though the line 8 check box is based on an outstanding home mortgage and nonqualifying use.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: 'Check the box on line 8 if you had one or more home mortgages in 2025 with an outstanding balance and you didn't use all of your home mortgage proceeds from those loans to buy, build, or substantially improve your home.'
findings.fix: Gate on whether the filer had a home mortgage outstanding in 2025, not whether interest was paid or entered on line 8a.

locators: p. 8, Line 8, "Interest paid on home mortgage proceeds used for other purposes isn’t deductible on lines 8a or 8b"
p. 8, Line 8a, "Enter on line 8a mortgage interest and points reported to you on Form 1098"
Schedule A (2025), lines 1–18

findings.who: A tenant-stockholder in a cooperative housing corporation who pays a monthly maintenance charge that includes the cooperative's real estate taxes; the filer owns shares and a proprietary lease, not the building or land.
findings.why_no: They read 'own a home or other real estate' as legal ownership of real property, answer No, and the property-tax line is treated as zero.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6, Line 5b: 'Enter on line 5b the state and local taxes you paid on real estate you own...'; p. 8: 'A home can be a house, condominium, cooperative, mobile home, boat, or similar property.'
findings.fix: Treat a cooperative housing corporation tenant-stockholder as owning a home for this gate; ask about co-op maintenance and split out the deductible real estate tax share.

findings.who: A tenant-stockholder in a cooperative housing corporation who pays a share of the cooperative's mortgage interest through maintenance; the filer receives no Form 1098 showing that interest.
findings.why_no: They answer No to owning a home or real estate; the follow-up asks only about a boat, camper, mobile home, or a mortgage on a home in another person's name, so the tool never asks whether they paid co-op mortgage interest not reported on their own Form 1098.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: 'A home can be a house, condominium, cooperative, mobile home, boat, or similar property'; Line 8b: 'If you paid home mortgage interest to a recipient who didn’t provide you a Form 1098, report your deductible mortgage interest on line 8b.'
findings.fix: Include cooperative housing in the gate and ask about co-op mortgage interest not reported on the filer's own Form 1098; a Yes should trigger the refusal.

findings.who: A surviving spouse who in 2025 pays mortgage interest on a home titled solely in the deceased spouse's name; a Form 1098 for the loan is issued in the survivor's name.
findings.why_no: They answer No to owning a home or real estate. They read the follow-up as asking whether the mortgage is in another person's name; because the mortgage/Form 1098 is in the survivor's name, they answer No even though the home is the decedent's and they paid the interest.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8, Line 8: 'A surviving spouse may deduct mortgage interest they pay after the decedent’s death.'
findings.fix: Ask directly about mortgage interest paid on a deceased spouse's home and treat it as within the home gate, regardless of whose name is on the mortgage or Form 1098.

findings.who: A co-borrower who is liable for and paid mortgage interest on a home titled in the other co-borrower's name, or a contract-for-deed buyer whose seller still holds title; the Form 1098 went to the other person or was not issued to the filer.
findings.why_no: They answer No to owning a home or real estate. They read the follow-up 'mortgage on a home in the name of another person' as asking whether the mortgage itself is in another person's name; because they are on the mortgage or the Form 1098 is shared, they answer No and the unreported-interest refusal is skipped.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8, Line 8a: 'Shared interest reported on someone else's Form 1098. ... report your share of the interest on line 8b'; p. 9, Line 8b: 'Seller financed mortgage. If you paid home mortgage interest to the person from whom you bought the home and that person didn’t provide you a Form 1098...'
findings.fix: Reword the follow-up to ask whether the filer paid interest on a home whose deed or Form 1098 is in someone else's name, including a co-borrower or seller; do not require the mortgage itself to be solely in another's name.

findings.who: A grantor of a revocable living trust, or sole member of a disregarded LLC, that holds the filer's home; the trust/LLC sold the home in 2025 and it had been financed with a qualified mortgage bond or the filer claimed the mortgage interest credit.
findings.why_no: The filer answers No to owning a home or other real estate because legal title is in the trust/LLC, and if no mortgage interest was paid in the filer's own name the gate is false, so the recapture question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 113, Line 17b: 'If you sold your home in 2025 and it was financed (in whole or in part) from the proceeds of any tax-exempt qualified mortgage bond or you claimed the mortgage interest credit, you may owe a recapture tax on the mortgage subsidy.'
findings.fix: Ask who is treated as owner for federal income tax, including grantor trusts and disregarded entities; include beneficial ownership in the home gate.

findings.who: An owner of a deeded timeshare interval who pays a property-tax share through the timeshare association and does not think of the interval as a home or other real estate.
findings.why_no: They read 'home or other real estate' as a primary or second home or land, not a vacation timeshare, and answer No, so the property-tax amount is treated as zero.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6, Line 5b: 'Enter on line 5b the state and local taxes you paid on real estate you own that wasn't used for business...'
findings.fix: Clarify that other real estate includes a deeded timeshare or vacation interval and ask whether the property-tax share is separately stated.

findings.who: A filer who pays medical or dental bills for a dependent, for a child the other parent claims under the divorced/separated-parent rules, or for a person who would be a dependent but for income or a joint return, and whose own and spouse's costs are not over 7.5%.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) paid yourselves'; the filer reads that as only the filer's and spouse's own care, not the qualifying dependents and other persons whose bills line 1 allows.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p.2: 'You can include medical and dental bills you paid in 2025 for anyone who was one of the following ... All dependents you claim ... Your child whom you don't claim ... Any person you could have claimed as a dependent ... except that person received $5,200 or more ... or filed a joint return.'
findings.fix: Ask about expenses paid for the filer, spouse, dependents, divorced/separated-parent child, and any person who would be a dependent but for the $5,200/joint-return/other-dependent rules.

findings.who: A filer whose adjusted gross income is lower than gross income (for example, from a deductible IRA/HSA contribution or self-employed health insurance) and whose medical costs exceed 7.5% of AGI but not 7.5% of gross income.
findings.why_no: The gate asks about 7.5% of 'your income,' not adjusted gross income; the filer uses gross income and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p.1: 'You can deduct only the part of your medical and dental expenses that exceeds 7.5% of the amount of your adjusted gross income on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 11b.'
findings.fix: Use 'adjusted gross income (Form 1040 line 11b)' and, on a joint return, joint AGI.

findings.who: A filer who in 2025 received an insurance reimbursement for medical expenses paid in an earlier year and subtracts that reimbursement from 2025 medical costs, dropping below 7.5%.
findings.why_no: The gate says to use costs 'after anything insurance paid'; the filer subtracts the 2025 reimbursement even though it relates to an earlier year.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p.2: 'If you received a reimbursement in 2025 for prior year medical or dental expenses, don't reduce your 2025 expenses by this amount.'
findings.fix: Tell the filer to reduce only by insurance or other reimbursements for the same 2025 expenses, not by prior-year reimbursements.

findings.who: An executor filing the final individual return of a taxpayer who died in 2025, where the decedent's estate paid medical or dental expenses that Publication 502 allows on the final return.
findings.why_no: The gate asks for costs 'you (or ... your spouse) paid yourselves'; the executor/decedent did not pay them personally, so the answer is no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p.1: 'Certain medical expenses paid out of a deceased taxpayer's estate can be claimed on the deceased taxpayer's final return.'
findings.fix: Add a condition for a decedent's final return and estate-paid expenses allowed by Publication 502.

findings.who: A filer whose health insurance is Medicare Part B/D deducted from tax-free Social Security benefits, or who pays otherwise-includible health insurance premiums with borrowed funds or a gift, and has no other medical costs over 7.5%.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether health insurance was paid for with money already taxed. Tax-free Social Security, borrowed funds, or a gift were not already taxed, so the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p.1: 'Insurance premiums for medical and dental care... The supplemental part of Medicare insurance (Medicare Part B). The premiums you pay for Medicare Part D insurance.' The source-based exclusions listed are pretax payroll, HSA/Archer MSA, retired public safety tax-free distributions, and PTC/APTC.
findings.fix: Ask whether the filer paid otherwise-includible health insurance premiums, then exclude only the specific tax-free/pretax sources; do not require the source to have been already taxed.

findings.who: A Marketplace enrollee whose APTC covered the premiums, who had to repay excess APTC, and who has no after-tax premium payment; other medical costs are below 7.5%.
findings.why_no: The filer did not pay health insurance premiums with money already taxed; the extra amount is an excess APTC repayment, so the filer answers no to the insurance question.
findings.irs_text: p502 p.12: 'However, any amount of advance payments of the premium tax credit that you did have to pay back can be included in medical expenses.' i8962 p.2: 'You cannot deduct the portion ... paid for by the PTC or APTC (after you determine how much of any excess APTC you must repay).'
findings.fix: Gate on Marketplace coverage/Form 1095-A/APTC reconciliation, not only after-tax premiums; ask about excess APTC repaid.

findings.who: A filer whose employer-sponsored health insurance premiums (or employer-plan medical expenses) are included in box 1 of Form W-2, and who has no separately paid after-tax premiums.
findings.why_no: The filer reads 'you paid yourselves' and 'health insurance paid for with money already taxed' as excluding employer-paid coverage, so says no even though box 1 makes it includible.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p.2: 'don't include on line 1 insurance premiums paid by an employer-sponsored health insurance plan (cafeteria plan) unless the premiums are included in box 1 of your Form(s) W-2. Also, don't include any other medical and dental expenses paid by the plan unless the amount paid is included in box 1.'
findings.fix: Ask about premiums or plan-paid expenses included in W-2 box 1, even if the employer paid the insurer.

findings.who: A filer who pays qualified long-term care insurance premiums with after-tax money and does not treat LTC insurance as 'health insurance'; other medical costs are below 7.5%.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'health insurance'; the filer thinks LTC coverage is not health insurance and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p.1: 'Insurance premiums for medical and dental care, including premiums for qualified long-term care insurance contracts as defined in Pub. 502.' p.2 gives the age-based limits ($480 to $6,020).
findings.fix: Mention qualified long-term care insurance premiums and the age limits in the gate/help.

findings.who: A filer whose out-of-pocket medical care costs are below 7.5% but whose medical travel, parking, tolls, ambulance, or limited lodging expenses push the total over 7.5%.
findings.why_no: The gate asks about 'medical and dental costs'; the filer does not count travel or lodging as medical/dental costs and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p.1-2: 'Ambulance service and other travel costs to get medical care... 21 cents a mile. Add parking and tolls...' 'Lodging expenses (but not meals) while away from home to receive medical care... Don't deduct more than $50 a night...'
findings.fix: Ask broadly about medical expenses as defined in Pub. 502, including travel/lodging, or list these examples in the gate.

findings.who: A married filer filing separately whose spouse has not filed or decided yet, or whose spouse first filed with the standard deduction and later amends to itemize. This concerns the gated question, not the computed gate, which matches line 12b exactly.
findings.why_no: The present tense 'Is your husband or wife itemizing' invites a no when the spouse has not yet chosen. 'Ask them if you do not know' does not say the answer must match the spouse's final return.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 33, Line 12b: "If your filing status is married filing separately and your spouse itemizes deductions on their return, check the box on line 12b"; p. 34: "your standard deduction is zero"
findings.fix: Ask 'Will your husband or wife itemize deductions on their 2025 return (including an amended return)?' Add to the help: 'If they have not decided, you must agree. If one of you itemizes, the other must too. If they later amend to itemize, you must amend as well.'

findings.who: A married-filing-separately filer whose spouse had no 2025 income, filed no 2025 return, and was born before January 2, 1961 or blind, but who itemized deductions on a separate 2024 return.
findings.why_no: The gate/helper says only 'spouse itemizing' without a year; the filer reads it as asking about the last return they know about and answers that the spouse itemized, so the computed condition is false and the gated question is skipped.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 33, Line 12d: 'you can check the appropriate box(es) on line 12d if your spouse had no income, isn't filing a return, and can't be claimed as a dependent'; p. 34, Exception 2 applies when 'your spouse itemizes deductions on their return'.
findings.fix: Add 'for 2025' to the gate/helper and ask whether the spouse filed a 2025 separate return with Schedule A itemized deductions; only a 2025 itemizing return should make the gate false.

findings.who: A married-filing-separately filer whose only mortgage interest goes on line 8b, not line 8a. Examples are seller-financed debt with no Form 1098, or interest on a loan shared with someone whose name is on the Form 1098. The mortgage debt is over $375,000.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed as 'Home mortgage interest is entered on line 8a' and MFS, so it is false. The question is never asked and the line is set to no, even though the debt limit applies equally to interest on line 8b.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8, Line 8b: "report your deductible mortgage interest on line 8b. Your deductible mortgage interest may be less than what you paid if one or more of the limits on home mortgage interest apply to you"; Shared interest: "If the shared interest was reported on the other person's Form 1098, report your share of the interest on line 8b"
findings.fix: Compute the gate as home mortgage interest (or points) entered on line 8a, 8b, or 8c, and married filing separately. Do not base it on line 8a alone.

findings.who: An MFS filer with a $300,000 mortgage on the house who also owes $100,000 on a boat, motor home, or mobile home with sleeping, toilet, and cooking facilities that serves as a second home. Or a filer whose only home is a cooperative apartment financed by a share loan.
findings.why_no: The question asks about 'the loans on your home' and the help says 'a second home'. A filer reads 'home' as a house or condo. They do not count a boat or RV loan, or a co-op share loan secured by stock, so they total $300,000 and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8, Line 8: "A home can be a house, condominium, cooperative, mobile home, boat, or similar property. It must provide basic living accommodations including sleeping space, toilet, and cooking facilities."
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Count every loan secured by your main home or a second home. A home can be a house, condo, co-op, mobile home, boat, or RV with sleeping, toilet, and cooking facilities.'

findings.who: An MFS filer with a $300,000 first mortgage and a $90,000 home equity line of credit, or a 'personal' or 'business' loan secured by the house.
findings.why_no: The filer thinks of 'the loans on your home' as the mortgage only. They leave out a HELOC, or a loan the lender labeled as something other than a mortgage, and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8, Line 8: "A home mortgage is any loan that is secured by your main home or second home, regardless of how the loan is labeled. It includes first and second mortgages, home equity loans, and refinanced mortgages."
findings.fix: Reword the question: 'Did all loans secured by your homes, including second mortgages, home equity loans and lines of credit, however labeled, add up to more than $375,000 at any time in 2025, or to more than the home is worth?'

findings.who: An MFS filer with two homes. A second home worth $150,000 carries $180,000 of loans, and the main home has ample equity. The total debt is under $375,000.
findings.why_no: The question says 'more than the home is worth', in the singular. The filer compares total loans with the combined value of both homes, or with the main home only, and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8, Limit when loans exceed the fair market value of the home: "If the total amount of all mortgages is more than the fair market value of the home, see Pub. 936"
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Check each home on its own: are the loans on that home more than that home is worth?'

locators: p. 8, Limits on home mortgage interest, "deduct home mortgage interest on up to $750,000 ($375,000 if you are married filing separately) of that debt"

p. 8, Limits on home mortgage interest, "you can only deduct home mortgage interest on up to $1,000,000 ($500,000 if you are married filing separately) of that debt", "deduct home mortgage interest on up to $750,000 ($375,000 if you are married filing separately) of that debt", "If the total amount of all mortgages is more than the fair market value of the home"

findings.who: A married couple filing separately. One spouse paid interest, reported on Form 1098, on a $500,000 mortgage on their main home.
findings.why_no: The gate is false for every married-filing-separately return, so the question is never asked. The gated line is set to no even though the separate-return limits ($375,000, or $500,000 for older debt) are the lowest of all.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: "you can only deduct home mortgage interest on up to $750,000 ($375,000 if you are married filing separately) of that debt"; "$1,000,000 ($500,000 if you are married filing separately)"
findings.fix: Ask every return with home mortgage interest. Compare the debt with $375,000 / $500,000 for married filing separately and $750,000 / $1,000,000 otherwise, or refuse every separate return that has home mortgage interest.

findings.who: A filer whose only home mortgage interest goes on line 8b: a $900,000 seller-financed note with no Form 1098, or a co-borrower's share shown on someone else's Form 1098, or a co-op tenant-stockholder's share of interest that was not on a 1098.
findings.why_no: The gate requires interest entered on line 8a, which holds only Form 1098 amounts. With nothing on 8a the gate is false and the debt limit is never tested.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8, Line 8b: "Your deductible mortgage interest may be less than what you paid if one or more of the limits on home mortgage interest apply to you."
findings.fix: Make the gate true when home mortgage interest is entered on line 8a or line 8b (and line 8c points), not only line 8a.

findings.who: A joint return. The filer's main home has a $600,000 mortgage, and the spouse alone holds a $250,000 mortgage on a vacation condo, or brought that mortgage into the marriage.
findings.why_no: The question says "the loans on your home". The filer counts only their own home and loans and answers no, although the joint limit applies to the combined debt.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: "A home mortgage is any loan that is secured by your main home or second home"; "deduct home mortgage interest on up to $750,000 ... of that debt"
findings.fix: "Did the loans on your or your spouse's main home and second home, all added together, come to more than $750,000 at any time in 2025?"

findings.who: A filer with a $700,000 house mortgage and a $120,000 loan on a liveaboard boat, RV or mobile home that has sleeping, toilet and cooking facilities and is used as a second home.
findings.why_no: "Loans on your home" and "a second home" read as houses. The filer does not count the boat or RV loan as a home loan, so the total seems to stay under $750,000.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: "A home can be a house, condominium, cooperative, mobile home, boat, or similar property. It must provide basic living accommodations including sleeping space, toilet, and cooking facilities."
findings.fix: Add to the help: "A second home can be a boat, RV, mobile home, condo or co-op with sleeping, toilet and cooking facilities. Count home equity loans and lines of credit too."

findings.who: A filer with a main home worth well above its loans and a second home whose $300,000 loan is more than its $250,000 value, or a filer who compares the loan with the purchase price or the tax assessment instead of today's market value.
findings.why_no: "More than the home is worth" uses the singular and gives no measure of worth. The filer nets both homes together, or uses the purchase price or assessed value, and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: "If the total amount of all mortgages is more than the fair market value of the home, see Pub. 936 to figure your deduction."
findings.fix: "Were the loans on either home, counted home by home, more than that home's market value (what it would sell for, not what you paid or its assessed value) at any time in 2025?"

findings.who: A filer whose $900,000 loan was taken out in 2016 and refinanced in 2020 at a higher balance, or who has some debt from before December 15, 2017 and some from after.
findings.why_no: The help says the limit is $1,000,000 "if all of it was borrowed on or before December 15, 2017." The filer may treat the refinance as a pre-2017 loan, use the $1,000,000 limit, and answer no, although the extra amount borrowed in the refinance is new debt under the $750,000 limit.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 8: "the $750,000 limit for debt taken out after December 15, 2017, is reduced by the amount of your qualifying debt subject to the $1,000,000 limit"
findings.fix: Add to the help: "A refinance counts as borrowed before December 15, 2017 only up to the balance it replaced. If any loan was taken out or increased after that date, use $750,000."

findings.who: A filer who paid a yearly personal property tax to a U.S. territory, such as Puerto Rico, on a car or other property.
findings.why_no: The main gate help says a U.S. territory's tax counts, so they answer Yes. The follow-up helper asks only whether they paid a 'state or local tax'; a territory tax is not a state or local tax, so they truthfully answer No and the line is zeroed.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3: 'Include taxes imposed by a U.S. territory with your state and local taxes on lines 5a, 5b, and 5c.'
findings.fix: Make the follow-up say 'state, local, or U.S. territory tax' or remove the redundant follow-up and use the main gate.

findings.who: A filer whose yearly car registration charge is partly based on the car's value and partly on weight or a flat amount.
findings.why_no: The main help says any part based on value is Yes, but the follow-up helper asks whether the tax is 'based on the value of the property' without saying 'any part'; the filer reads that as requiring the whole charge to be value-based and answers No.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6: 'You can deduct only the part of the fee that was based on the car's value.'
findings.fix: Use 'any part of the charge was based on value' in the follow-up, as the main help does.

findings.who: A filer who paid a yearly value-based personal property tax on property other than a car or boat, such as a mobile home, aircraft, or other tangible personal property.
findings.why_no: The follow-up helper gives only 'such as a car or a boat' and omits the main gate's 'other belongings'; the filer reads the list as limited to cars and boats and answers No.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6: 'Enter on line 5c the state and local personal property taxes you paid, but only if the taxes were based on value alone and were imposed on a yearly basis.'
findings.fix: Say 'personal property, such as a car, boat, or other belongings' in the follow-up.

findings.who: A filer who in 2025 paid a personal property tax bill that was for 2024 or another prior year and was assessed before 2026.
findings.why_no: They read 'In 2025' as asking about a 2025 tax year bill, not about a payment made in 2025 for an earlier year's bill, and answer No.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 7: 'Only taxes paid in 2025 and assessed prior to 2026 can be deducted for 2025.'
findings.fix: Add 'including a prior year's bill paid in 2025' or ask about payments made during 2025.

findings.who: A filer who sold or disposed of the car or boat before 2025 but paid a delinquent personal property tax bill on it in 2025.
findings.why_no: They read 'on a car, a boat' as requiring current ownership and answer No because they no longer own the property.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 7: 'Only taxes paid in 2025 and assessed prior to 2026 can be deducted for 2025.'
findings.fix: Say 'even if you no longer own the property' or ask about tax paid on property you formerly owned.

findings.who: A filer who paid a U.S. territory personal property tax that is partly allocable to excluded income and partly not.
findings.why_no: They read the gated question's help 'unless it belongs to income left out of this return' as excluding the whole territory tax and answer No, missing the non-excluded part.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3: 'However, don't include any U.S. territory taxes you paid that are allocable to excluded income.'
findings.fix: Clarify that only the allocable excluded part is omitted; answer Yes if any part is not allocable to excluded income.

locators: Schedule A (2025), lines 1–18

p. 3, U.S. territory taxes, "Include taxes imposed by a U.S. territory with your state and local taxes on lines 5a, 5b, and 5c", "However, don't include any U.S. territory taxes you paid that are allocable to excluded income"; p. 6, Line 5c, "Enter on line 5c the state and local personal property taxes you paid, but only if the taxes were based on value alone and were imposed on a yearly basis", "You can deduct only the part of the fee that was based on the car's value"; p. 7, "Only taxes paid in 2025 and assessed prior to 2026 can be deducted for 2025"

findings.who: A filer who owns a rental house, or uses part of a home or a parcel in a business, and enters the total property tax from the county bills, including the tax on the rental or business portion.
findings.why_no: The question defines 'not deductible' by a list after a colon: foreign real estate, service charges, improvements, tax charged to the buyer, refunds, and tax not assessed before 2026. Business or rental use is not on the list, so the truthful answer to the question as worded is no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6, Line 5b: "Enter on line 5b the state and local taxes you paid on real estate you own that wasn't used for business"
findings.fix: Add to the list: 'tax on real estate, or the part of a property, used in a business or rented out (this tax belongs on Schedule C, E, or F).' Better, ask about business or rental use as its own yes/no question before the list, and say the list is not complete.

findings.who: A filer whose bill includes a levy that is not assessed uniformly at a like rate on all property in the community, or whose proceeds do not go to general governmental purposes. Examples are a special-district or benefit assessment on certain parcels only that is not plainly for an 'improvement', or a fee for a private association that the bill collects.
findings.why_no: The charge is not foreign, not an itemized service charge, and not visibly an improvement, so it matches nothing on the list, and the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6, Line 5b: "but only if the taxes are assessed uniformly at a like rate on all real property throughout the community, and the proceeds are used for general community or governmental purposes"
findings.fix: Add to the list: 'any charge not levied at the same rate on all property in the community, or not used for general government purposes (for example, a special assessment on some parcels only, or an association fee).'

findings.who: A filer who paid the property tax on real estate they do not own, such as a parent's or adult child's house, and included it in the amount entered.
findings.why_no: The list does not mention ownership. The tax was paid and is a genuine local real estate tax, so nothing on the list applies.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6, Line 5b: "the state and local taxes you paid on real estate you own"
findings.fix: Add to the list: 'tax on real estate that you (or your spouse) do not own.'

findings.who: A filer with an escrow account who enters the escrow deposits for taxes, or the annual escrow total from the lender statement, rather than the amount the lender actually paid to the taxing authority in 2025.
findings.why_no: The filer sees the escrow deposits as 'real estate tax' and nothing on the list covers the gap between deposits and disbursements, so they answer no. The excess deposits are then deducted.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6, Line 5b: "If your mortgage payments include your real estate taxes, you can include only the amount the mortgage company actually paid to the taxing authority in 2025."
findings.fix: State on the amount question, or add to the list: 'escrow money your lender held but did not pay to the taxing authority in 2025 (use the taxes paid shown on Form 1098 or the escrow statement).'

findings.who: Joint filers where only the spouse owns real estate (for example, a premarital house or inherited land), and the spouse's property tax reaches the return's real estate tax amount.
findings.why_no: The parent helper reads 'You owned a home or other real estate, or paid interest on a loan secured by a home'. The filer answers for themself, says no, and the leave-out question is never asked for the spouse's foreign, service, or improvement charges.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6, Line 5b: "Don't include the following amounts on line 5b. • Foreign taxes you paid on real estate."
findings.fix: Reword the parent as 'You or your spouse owned a home or other real estate in 2025, or paid interest on a loan secured by a home.' Alternatively, condition the gate on a non-zero real estate tax amount rather than on ownership.

findings.who: A filer who prepaid in December 2025 a tax bill their locality issued before the tax is legally assessed under state law, for example an early or estimated bill for the 2026 levy.
findings.why_no: The help says 'Tax is billed when it is assessed under state or local law.' The filer had a bill before 2026, so they conclude the tax was assessed before 2026 and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6, Prepayment of next year's property taxes: "Only taxes paid in 2025 and assessed prior to 2026 can be deducted for 2025. State or local law determines whether and when a property tax is assessed, which is generally when the taxpayer becomes liable for the property tax imposed."
findings.fix: Replace the help sentence with: 'A tax is assessed when state or local law makes you liable for it, which may differ from when you are billed. A payment in 2025 toward next year's tax that your state had not yet assessed is not deductible.'

findings.who: A filer who bought a home in 2025 and, at closing, paid real estate tax covering part of the year before the purchase date (the seller's share), shown on the settlement statement.
findings.why_no: The list mentions only 'tax charged to the buyer on a sale', which a buyer reads as tax they themselves paid, or as a seller-only item. Nothing tells them that tax for the seller's part of the year is not their deduction, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 6, Line 5b: "Any real estate taxes you paid at closing should be shown on your settlement statement." together with "the state and local taxes you paid on real estate you own"
findings.fix: Add: 'If you bought real estate, any tax you paid at closing for the part of the year before you owned it (see your settlement statement).'

locators: p. 6, Line 5b, "Don't include the following amounts on line 5b", "Foreign taxes you paid on real estate"
p. 6, Line 5b, "Don't include the following amounts on line 5b", "Itemized charges for services to specific property or persons"

findings.who: A retiree or other filer with no wages whose state income tax was withheld only from a pension or IRA distribution (Form 1099-R), unemployment benefits (Form 1099-G), gambling winnings (Form W-2G), or contractor pay (Form 1099-NEC/1099-MISC).
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether state or local tax was 'taken out of your ... pay' and points to Form W-2 boxes 17 and 19. A pension, an unemployment check, or a jackpot is not 'pay', and they have no W-2, so the truthful answer is no. Even after a yes, the gated question adds only W-2 boxes 17 and 19.
findings.line: sa.line5a_if_state_tax (and through it Schedule A line 5a), unless another input captures non-W-2 withholding
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3, Line 5a: "State and local income taxes withheld from your salary during 2025. Your Form(s) W-2 will show these amounts. Forms W-2G, 1099-G, 1099-R, 1099-MISC, and 1099-NEC may also show state and local income taxes withheld"
findings.fix: Broaden the gate: 'In 2025, was state or local income tax withheld from any payment to you (or, on a joint return, your spouse), such as pay (Form W-2 boxes 17 and 19), a pension or IRA distribution (Form 1099-R), unemployment benefits (Form 1099-G), gambling winnings (Form W-2G), or nonemployee pay (Form 1099-NEC or 1099-MISC)?' Ask for each form's state and local withholding box. Keep the exclusion for tax deducted on Schedule C, E, or F. If a separate input already collects non-W-2 withholding, say so in this help text.

findings.who: An employee in California, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island or Washington whose pay had mandatory state disability, family leave, or unemployment fund contributions withheld (often shown in W-2 box 14 as SDI, FLI, DBL, or UI/WF/SWF), but no state income tax.
findings.why_no: These contributions are not 'income tax' and are not in boxes 17 or 19, so the filer answers no. That is correct for this line, but if the tool has no other input for these contributions, the 5a amount is lost.
findings.line: Schedule A line 5a component reached only through this gate (if no separate input exists for mandatory state fund contributions)
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3, Line 5a: "Mandatory contributions you made to the California, New Jersey, or New York Nonoccupational Disability Benefit Fund ... Mandatory contributions to the Alaska, California, New Jersey, or Pennsylvania state unemployment fund. Mandatory contributions to state family leave programs"
findings.fix: Ask a separate ungated question about mandatory state disability, family leave, or unemployment fund contributions withheld from pay (often in W-2 box 14), or add to this gate's help: 'State disability (SDI), family leave (FLI), and state unemployment contributions in box 14 are asked separately.'

findings.who: A worker whose local tax is called a 'wage tax', 'earned income tax', or 'school district tax' (for example, the Philadelphia wage tax, Pennsylvania EIT, or an Ohio school district tax), or whose employer reports it in box 14 rather than box 19.
findings.why_no: The filer does not see a 'wage tax' or an amount in box 14 as 'income tax' or as box 19, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3, Line 5a: "State and local income taxes withheld from your salary during 2025."; fw2 p. 4: "19 Local income tax"
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Include local taxes on wages, such as city wage taxes, earned income taxes, or school district income taxes, even if your employer shows them in box 14 instead of box 19.'

findings.who: A filer whose only state payroll contribution is a mandatory Washington State Supplemental Workmen's Compensation Fund contribution taken from pay; they have no state or local income tax payment and no disability, unemployment, or family leave contribution.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about paying state or local income tax not taken from pay or paying into a state disability, unemployment, or family leave fund. Workers' compensation is not named, and the help lists only SDI, SUI, and FLI, so the filer truthfully answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3, Line 5a: 'Mandatory contributions ... Washington State Supplemental Workmen's Compensation Fund.'
findings.fix: Add workers' compensation funds to the gate and help, e.g., '...state disability, unemployment, workers' compensation, or family leave fund,' or ask broadly about any mandatory state payroll fund contribution.

findings.who: A filer who made a charitable gift and received a local (not state) tax credit, then applied that credit against local income tax; they did not pay the tax in cash.
findings.why_no: The gate's help names only 'a state tax credit for a charity gift.' The filer reads that as excluding local credits, and the main question asks about paying tax, so applying a local credit is not a payment.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3: 'to the extent you apply the state or local tax credit to this or a prior year's state or local tax liability, you may include this amount on line 5a, 5b, or 5c...'
findings.fix: Change the help to 'state or local tax credit for a charity gift' and add local credits to the gate examples.

findings.who: A filer who in 2025 applied a state or local tax credit received for a charitable gift to their prior year's (e.g., 2024) state or local income tax liability, rather than to 2025 tax.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether in 2025 they paid state or local income tax, and the help says the credit was 'applied to your tax' but does not say a prior year's liability. The filer reads 'your tax' as the 2025 tax and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3: 'to the extent you apply the state or local tax credit to this or a prior year's state or local tax liability, you may include this amount on line 5a, 5b, or 5c...'
findings.fix: Ask whether in 2025 the filer applied a state or local charitable tax credit to this year's or a prior year's state or local tax liability, and state that prior-year applications count.

findings.who: A filer with state income tax withheld from an annuity or other 1099-R distribution that is not a pension or IRA (for example, a commercial annuity or profit-sharing distribution).
findings.why_no: The help names 'a pension, IRA' but not annuities or other 1099-R distributions. The filer reads the list as complete and, because the tax was taken out rather than paid directly, answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca p. 3, Line 5a: 'Forms W-2G, 1099-G, 1099-R, 1099-MISC, and 1099-NEC may also show state and local income taxes withheld.'
findings.fix: Name 1099-R distributions, including annuities and other retirement distributions, or replace the list with 'tax withheld from any other income.'
